newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada bonds close much stronger on inflation data.
newsitem.headline: Canada bonds close much stronger on inflation data.

text.p: Canadian bonds closed much stronger on Friday, pulled higher by a rally in U.S. Treasuries following the release of weaker-than-expected U.S. economic data, analysts said.

"The retail sales and consumer price numbers out of the U.S. were much more market-friendly than expected. As a result the U.S. market took off," said Michael Gregory, economist and strategist with Lehman Brothers. "We went along for the ride."
Canada's 8.0 percent bond due 2023 rose C$1.10 to C$102.50 to yield 7.775 percent. The U.S. 30-year benchmark rose 1-18/32 to yield 6.95 percent.
The spread between the benchmark bonds widened to 83 basis points from 80 basis points at Thursday's close.

Both Canadian and U.S. fixed income markets rallied following the release of the U.S. data, which showed consumer prices in August rose a lower-than-expected 0.1 percent. The U.S. Commerce Department reported August retail sales rose 0.2 percent, also below expectations.

The data sparked a sharp rally in fixed-income markets, persuading many investors that the U.S. Federal Reserve's rate setting committee will not hike rates when it meets on September 24, analysts said.

Canadian consumer price index data out this morning had a lesser impact on the Canadian market, dealers said. Statistics Canada reported core inflation rose just 0.1 percent on the month and 1.3 percent on the year.

The Canadian market also saw issues from two borrowers set this morning. Metro Toronto issued a C$100 million 7.4 percent bond due September 27, 2006 with CIBC Wood Gundy Securities Inc as lead manager. Metro Toronto issued a C$75 million 8.0 percent bond due September 27, 2016.
Canada Mortgage and Housing Corp also came to market with a C$500 million 6.25 percent bond due January 2, 2002.
The lead manager of the CMHC issue was RBC Dominion Securities Inc.
In other prices, the 7.0 percent of 2006 rose C$0.95 to C$98.10 to yield 7.265 percent. The U.S. 10-year benchmark rose 1-1/32 to yield 6.73 percent.
The spread between the two bonds widened to 54 basis points from 53 basis points at the close of trading on Thursday.
The three-month cash bill traded at 3.74 percent against the U.S. three-month bill at 5.20 percent.
